title: Llovía y llovió
titleEn: It was raining and it rained
blurbEn: In literature the imperfect stops being a rule and becomes an instrument.
body:
En literatura, la diferencia entre imperfecto e indefinido deja de ser una regla y se convierte en un instrumento.

«Llovía» abre una escena. «Llovió» la cierra. Un autor puede empezar un capítulo con imperfectos —hacía frío, la casa estaba vacía, nadie hablaba— y mantener así al lector suspendido, sin que ocurra nada, todo el tiempo que quiera.

Después basta un indefinido para que el relato arranque: «entonces llamaron a la puerta».

Aprendí a ver esto leyendo, no estudiando. En los primeros meses el imperfecto me parecía simplemente el pasado de las descripciones. Ahora veo que es el tiempo del ambiente, y que un escritor lo usa para retrasar las cosas.

Hay novelas enteras escritas casi en imperfecto. Producen una sensación rara, como de recuerdo o de sueño.

Y hay otras, sobre todo policíacas, escritas en indefinido puro: pasó esto, luego esto, luego esto. Avanzan mucho y respiran poco.

Nunca se me habría ocurrido pensar en un tiempo verbal como en una decisión de estilo.

Es probablemente lo más interesante que he aprendido este año.
translationEn:
In literature, the difference between the imperfect and the preterite stops being a rule and becomes an instrument.

"Llovía" opens a scene. "Llovió" closes it. An author can begin a chapter with imperfects — it was cold, the house was empty, nobody was speaking — and hold the reader suspended like that, with nothing happening, for as long as they like.

Then a single preterite is enough for the story to get going: "then there was a knock at the door".

I learned to see this by reading, not by studying. In the early months the imperfect seemed to me simply the past tense of descriptions. Now I see it's the tense of atmosphere, and that a writer uses it to delay things.

There are whole novels written almost entirely in the imperfect. They produce a strange sensation, like a memory or a dream.

And there are others, detective novels especially, written in pure preterite: this happened, then this, then this. They move fast and breathe little.

It would never have occurred to me to think of a tense as a decision about style.

It's probably the most interesting thing I've learned this year.

Llovía.note: Opens a scene and holds it. Nothing has happened yet; the reader is waiting.

Llovió.note: Closes it. A completed event, and the narrative can move on.

phrases.gloss: They move fast and breathe little
